lede: A poor Hamburg double-bass player's son, announced to the world at twenty as the next great composer, who spent more than twenty years nerving himself to write a symphony in Beethoven's shadow, and then wrote four of the finest ever made.

ps: Johannes Brahms was born in Hamburg on 7 May 1833. In 1853 Robert Schumann hailed him in print as a genius, and he became a lifelong friend of Robert's wife, Clara.

He settled in Vienna in the 1860s and lived there for the rest of his life. His German Requiem (1868) made him famous, and from 1876 he wrote four symphonies, concertos, chamber music, piano pieces and about 200 songs, including the Lullaby known around the world.
In an age of musical revolutionaries he worked in the classical forms of Bach, Haydn and Beethoven, and made them new. He died in Vienna on 3 April 1897, less than a year after Clara.

His father, Johann Jakob, was a struggling musician who played double bass and horn in Hamburg's dance halls and theatres. His mother, Christiane, was a seamstress seventeen years older than her husband. The family lived in cramped rooms near the harbour.
He began piano at seven with Otto Cossel, who soon passed him to the best teacher in the city, Eduard Marxsen. Marxsen taught him free, grounding him in Bach and Beethoven.

As a teenager he helped the family by playing piano in taverns and restaurants at night and arranging light music for publishers under false names. He was a voracious reader and collected folk songs all his life.

1853: he toured as accompanist to the Hungarian violinist Ede Remenyi. In Hanover he met the great violinist Joseph Joachim, who became his closest musical friend. In Weimar he visited Liszt. On 30 September he knocked on the Schumanns' door in Dusseldorf. In October Robert published his article New Paths, naming the twenty-year-old as the chosen one.
1854 to 1856: after Robert's collapse he moved to Dusseldorf to help Clara and her children. His feelings for her ran deep; after Robert's death in 1856 they stayed devoted friends.

1859: his First Piano Concerto was hissed at its Leipzig performance. In 1860, with Joachim, he signed a public statement against the 'New German' school of Liszt and Wagner, which brought him ridicule.
1862 to 1863: he visited Vienna and began to make it his home, at first leading a choir there. In 1872 he took rooms at Karlsgasse 4 and kept them for 25 years.

1868: A German Requiem was first performed in Bremen Cathedral on Good Friday. He added a new fifth movement, making seven, for its full premiere in Leipzig in 1869. Its success made him the leading German composer of his generation.
1876: his First Symphony was finally played in Karlsruhe, about fourteen years after he sketched its first movement. The conductor Hans von Bulow called it 'Beethoven's Tenth'.

1877 to 1885: the Second, Third and Fourth Symphonies, the Violin Concerto for Joachim (1878), the Second Piano Concerto and the Academic Festival Overture, written to thank the University of Breslau for an honorary degree.

1890s: he said he would retire, then heard the clarinettist Richard Muhlfeld and wrote the Clarinet Trio, the Clarinet Quintet and two sonatas for him. In May 1896, as Clara lay dying after a stroke, he wrote the Four Serious Songs. He died of liver cancer on 3 April 1897.
A German Requiem, sung in German to Bible texts he chose himself. It is meant to comfort the living, not pray for the dead, and was shaped partly by his mother's death in 1865.
The four symphonies (1876 to 1885) and the two piano concertos, the Violin Concerto and the Double Concerto for violin and cello.
The Hungarian Dances (published from 1869), at first for piano duet, his most popular music in his lifetime, and the Wiegenlied, Op. 49 No. 4 (1868), the famous Lullaby.

Chamber music, perhaps his greatest strength: the Piano Quintet, the string sextets, the piano trios and quartets, and the late Clarinet Quintet. Also the Variations on a Theme by Handel and short late piano pieces.
Eduard Marxsen (1806 to 1887), his teacher, to whom he dedicated his Second Piano Concerto.
Robert Schumann (1810 to 1856), who announced him to the world in 1853.
Clara Schumann (1819 to 1896), his closest friend for 43 years.
Joseph Joachim (1831 to 1907), violinist, adviser on his string writing, and the soloist of his Violin Concerto.
Eduard Hanslick (1825 to 1904), Vienna's most powerful critic, his defender and friend.
Antonin Dvorak (1841 to 1904), the young Czech composer whom he recommended to his own publisher.
Richard Wagner (1813 to 1883), held up by critics as his opposite.

Vienna was the capital of the Habsburg Empire and of music, with new concert halls built in the 1860s and 1870s along the Ringstrasse. He conducted the concerts of the Society of the Friends of Music there from 1872 to 1875.

Musicians split into camps. One side, around Liszt and Wagner, called itself the 'music of the future' and favoured opera and music that told stories. The other, linked with Brahms and Hanslick, defended 'absolute' music in classical forms.
Germany was united in 1871. Brahms, a patriot, celebrated with his Triumphlied. He also studied old music deeply and helped edit early music, including Couperin's harpsichord pieces.
Bulow's phrase 'the three Bs', Bach, Beethoven and Brahms, set him in the line of the great masters.

In 1933, for the centenary of his birth, Arnold Schoenberg gave a talk later published as 'Brahms the Progressive'. He showed how Brahms's way of growing music from tiny motifs pointed to the twentieth century.
He never married. He lived simply and was generous in secret to his family and young musicians. He was buried in Vienna's Central Cemetery near Beethoven and Schubert.

myths.c: As a boy he played piano in brothels.
myths.t: Friends recalled him telling such stories in later life. Some historians think they were exaggerated, and others that he meant the rough dockside taverns where music and prostitution mixed. It cannot be proven either way.

myths.c: He and Clara Schumann were lovers.
myths.t: Their bond is clear and deep. They agreed to destroy many of their letters, so the true nature of the relationship cannot be known.

myths.c: Brahms and Wagner were at war.
myths.t: The war was mostly fought by critics and followers. Brahms admired much of Wagner's music and studied his scores, while Wagner attacked him in print only occasionally.

myths.c: He fell asleep while Liszt played to him.
myths.t: The story comes from the American pianist William Mason, who was there in 1853 but wrote it down nearly fifty years later. Liszt stayed courteous to Brahms afterwards.
